detailsHtml:
How the Guildrun tier list should be read

This Guildrun tier list ranks Demo 0.5.1 hero priority by job reliability, team fit, and how often a hero converts the current data into fight-winning value. It is not a claim that one hero is always correct. Shop offers, relics, items, ranks, fight mode, and enemy formation can move a hero up or down.

The useful question is not who is strongest in a vacuum? It is which hero fixes the next fight while keeping a real build path open? That is the filter used below.

Tier list scope

TierMeaningCurrent Demo read
SHigh-priority coreReliable job, strong scaling or survival, and easy links to common items/relics.
AStrong with a planExcellent when the board already supports the hero's trigger or target access.
BSituationalCorrect in specific comps, but weaker as a blind early pick.
INFERREDPatch-sensitiveRanking is based on Demo data and observed guide signals; verify after balance patches.

Demo and full-game differences

Demo tier lists should be treated as early signals. Demo 0.5.1 has known hero records, ranks, items, relics, and fight modes, but future patches can change costs, trigger values, hero availability, or full-game progression. If a later patch changes a hero's base ability or specialization, re-rank the job, not the name.

Best tier list categories

The cleanest way to use a tier list is by category. A tank anchor, shield engine, back-line carry, rush finisher, and economy piece are not competing for the same job. Do not drop a needed anchor just because a carry sits higher on a generic list.

Hero tiers

TierHeroesWhy they rank here
SPimenta, Pollen, Gustav, Aria, RowanThey give clear jobs: tanking, shields, debuffs, Stall scaling, or back-line magic payoff.
AKai, Reyna, Nyx, Tilly, Dragomir, Skorn, GraceStrong when supported by shields, Rush, Shards, Crit, poison, or late-fight survival.
BIrini, Zuri, Sal, Ratna, Hoyoung, Ming, Funke, Fiona, KarsuPlayable and sometimes correct, but more dependent on setup, items, or enemy layout.

Why Pimenta and Pollen sit high: they create useful time. Pimenta brings a front-line poison cloud and HP/S after Stall (15). Pollen adds poison, shields, and healing after Stall (15). Those are easy to understand, easy to build around, and useful before a perfect relic appears.

Why Aria and Gustav sit high: both convert protected time into area control. Aria brings Frost and Burn from range, while Gustav adds Frost damage and shields. They need protection, but their payoff is clear.

Comp and build tiers

Comp typePriority heroesWhen to play it
Shield and StallPimenta, Pollen, Gustav, Rowan, GraceWhen fights are lasting long enough for Stall 15 to 20 effects to resolve.
Rush pressureNyx, Reyna, Kai, Tilly, DragomirWhen target access is clean and early kills matter more than deep scaling.
Debuff controlAria, Pollen, Gustav, Skorn, PimentaWhen poison, Frost, Burn, or status relics are already appearing.
Shard economyTilly, Dragomir, NiklasWhen the run can convert extra Shards into ranks, items, or team size.

Use the strategy guide when you need full build routing. Use hero dossiers when a shop offers a hero you do not know. Use relic records before forcing a comp around a relic name.

When a lower tier hero becomes correct

A B-tier hero can be the correct buy when it completes a role, a duplicate rank, a dual-class path, or a mode-specific answer. Hoyoung is better when a fight needs low-health cleanup. Irini improves when attack-speed scaling and Stall timing are already protected. Zuri improves when the team can feed Crit and let her defensive scaling work.

  • Move a hero up if two or more owned pieces trigger the same payoff.
  • Move a hero down if it walks too long before acting.
  • Move a hero down if it requires a relic you do not own.
  • Move a hero up if the next enemy formation specifically rewards its range, control, or durability.

Tier list update rules

After every balance change, check four things before trusting any ranking: base ability text, specialization text, modifier pool, and mode pressure. If only one number changes, the tier may stay the same. If a trigger timing changes from Stall 15 to Stall 25, the whole build timing changes.

title: Guildrun Stall Guide: What Stall Means and How It Works
seoTitle: Guildrun Stall Guide: What Stall Means and How It Works
seoDescription: Guildrun stall guide explaining what Stall means, when Stall 10/15/20/35 triggers matter, which heroes use it, and why stall builds fail in Demo fights.
seoKeywords: how does stall work in guildrun
imageAlt: Guildrun stall guide image for Pimenta and delayed Stall trigger teams
excerpt: A direct explanation of Stall as a delayed combat trigger, which heroes use it, which timings matter, and why stall teams fail before payoff.
author: Frontline Pathfinder
quickSummary: Read Stall as a delayed combat threshold, not a button you press.
Protect the board until the first useful Stall timing actually resolves.
Use Stall Certainty, shields, taunts, and healing only when they solve the next fight.
commonMistakes: Building for Stall while the frontline dies before 10 to 15 seconds
Buying Stall pieces without a payoff hero already active
Ignoring target access because the team survived longer
Stacking delayed modifiers in Red Rift before stabilizing deaths
Treating every Stall number as equal when 10, 15, 20, and 35 seconds do different jobs
detailsHtml:
What stall means

In Guildrun, Stall is a delayed combat timing condition. When a hero, specialization, relic, or modifier says After Stall (15), it is asking the board to survive long enough for that delayed threshold to matter. It is not a manual cast button and it is not the same thing as playing slowly in the shop.

The exact implementation can move with Demo patches, so use the in-game wording first. In the current local Demo 0.5.1 data, Stall appears as timed thresholds such as 10, 15, 20, 30, 35, 40, 50, and 60 seconds, plus wording like On Stall trigger.

Simple definition

TermPractical meaningHow to read it during a fight
After Stall (10)A first delayed payoffThe board must avoid early collapse.
After Stall (15)Common sustain or damage breakpointPimenta, Pollen, and Irini start showing value here.
After Stall (20)Mid-fight conversion pointGrace resurrection, Pollen poison boost, Aria scaling, and several crit/shield paths become relevant.
After Stall (35)Deep survival breakpointSecond Wind can fully heal and refill mana, but only if the holder is alive.
On Stall triggerPayoff when a Stall checkpoint resolvesRepeated trigger wording rewards multiple Stall thresholds or faster trigger access.

Why stall matters

Stall is valuable because it converts time into stats, shields, healing, taunts, debuffs, or mana. That makes it strongest when the team already has a reason to survive longer: a poison cloud ticking, a shield engine scaling, a back-line mage channeling, or a tank gaining permanent defense.

The trap is obvious: a delayed payoff does nothing if the fight is already lost. Before buying a Stall modifier, watch the first 10 seconds of the failed combat. If the carry dies, the support is targeted first, or the tank never receives pressure, you have a formation problem before you have a Stall problem.

How stall works in practice

A reliable Stall plan has three parts: a front line that owns first contact, a payoff that activates at a known timing, and enough damage or debuff conversion to finish the fight after the delay. Surviving for 40 seconds without a kill plan is not a win condition.

Trigger or setup conditions

Hero or modifierStall hookUse case
PimentaPepper Spray gains HP/S after Stall (15)Front-line poison tank that rewards enemies staying inside the cloud.
PollenSanctuary heals after Stall (15), then upgrades at 20 and 40Mystic sustain field for poison, shields, and longer fights.
AriaThe Crescendo gains Magic on Stall trigger and upgrades at 20/40/60Back-line Mage scaling if the team can protect the channel.
RowanHearty gains HP/S after Stall (10)Defensive anchor for Tank and Vanguard teams.
GraceSalvation can resurrect after Stall (20)Late-fight recovery when the team can avoid immediate wipeout.
Stall CertaintyStall abilities trigger 6 seconds fasterBackup acceleration for Tank, Mystic, or Mage paths that already have payoff.
DistractionTaunts at Stall 10/20/30/40/50Repeated enemy control when the tank can survive being targeted.

Common stall mistakes

  • No early contact control. If the wrong hero is hit first, your Stall timer is irrelevant. Fix formation before buying another delayed modifier.
  • No payoff density. One Stall keyword on one hero is not a team engine. Pair tanks, Mystics, shields, poison, or Mage scaling so the timer creates multiple values.
  • No damage conversion. Pollen and Pimenta can keep a fight alive, but the run still needs a way to kill priority enemies.
  • Wrong mode timing. Red Rift punishes deaths. Endless rewards scaling. Do not use the same greed level in both modes.

How to build a Stall team

Start with the first death. If the board dies before 10 seconds, buy immediate durability or reposition. If it reaches 15 seconds but cannot finish, add damage conversion. If it reaches 20 seconds and stabilizes, then deeper Stall triggers become realistic.

Board needBetter Stall answerConnected page
First contactPimenta, Rowan, Skorn, or a true tank laneClass data
Team sustainPollen, Gustav, Grace, Shield Formation, Protective MagicShields
Delayed damageAria, Irini, poison stacks, Burn or Frost absorptionStatus effects
Mode pressureSafer pivots for Red Rift, scaling for EndlessFight modes

For a full run context, use the strategy guide. For exact stat rules, use the stats page. This Stall page should answer the mechanic quickly, not replace every hero dossier.

title: Guildrun Beginner Guide: First Run, Shop, and Positioning
imageAlt: Guildrun beginner guide showing the opening hero selection
excerpt: A complete first-run handbook for the Demo: run loop, role coverage, positioning, Shard spending, and how to learn from every loss.
author: Guildrun Guide Team
quickSummary: Stabilize a three-hero board before chasing synergy.
Spend Shards only on a named next-fight problem.
Use positioning and Rewind as learning tools, not restart buttons.
commonMistakes: Forcing one class before the shop supports it
Rerolling without naming an acceptable outcome
Copying one formation into every fight
Buying Team Size before the fourth hero has a job
Treating every loss as a damage problem
detailsHtml:
What Guildrun is asking you to do

Guildrun is a single-player PvE roguelike autobattler. You recruit heroes, choose items and relics, set formation and specializations, then let combat resolve automatically. The important skill is not clicking during the fight. It is reading what happened and spending the next reward on one specific weakness.

This guide is written for Demo 0.5.1. Use it once in order, then return to the section that matches the problem that ended your last run.

Your first complete run loop

A run begins with one of three hero-and-relic bundles and 15 spendable Shards. The opening only needs to survive the first fights; it does not have to lock the final build.

  1. Inspect the encounter. Check enemy range, abilities, formation, and any fight modifier before moving a hero.
  2. Choose the active board. Field three heroes at first, then expand toward five only when the new slot has a clear job.
  3. Predict first contact. Name the hero who should take the first attacks and the enemy your main damage dealer should reach.
  4. Watch the first failure. Record the first important death, interrupted cast, wasted walk, or target that survived too long.
  5. Spend for that failure. Buy durability, damage, mana, range, a duplicate, or a new role only when it changes the next fight.

Before leaving a shop, you should be able to explain what the purchase fixes. “More power” is not enough. “Fiona now casts before Pimenta drops below half health” is a useful answer.

Build a job-complete team first

A useful first-run framework is one hero that absorbs opening pressure, one reliable damage dealer, and a third piece that supports or scales those two. Specializations can move heroes beyond their starting roles, so treat classes as starting points rather than permanent identities.

JobWhat success looks likeFailure to watch
AnchorLives until allied abilities begin resolvingThe support or carry is targeted first
DamageReaches and finishes the priority targetWalks too long or attacks an irrelevant body
Support or controlCreates time before the formation collapsesCasts after the important death

Three early frameworks that stay readable

  • Shield and Stall. A durable front line buys time for delayed payoffs.
  • Direct damage. One carry with clean target access and enough protection to act twice.
  • Status control. Poison, Frost, or Burn when several pieces reward the same trigger.

Keep the fourth slot flexible until the engine is proven. The fifth slot should answer a matchup or multiply a trigger you already own.

Positioning before combat

Because combat resolves automatically, formation is how you influence the opening exchange. Positioning decides who receives pressure, which abilities reach their targets, and how long a carry has to scale.

Predict the normal target order

  1. Find the closest valid hero.
  2. If distance ties, use class priority: Tank, Vanguard, Warrior, Duelist, Assassin, Mage, then Mystic.
  3. If class also ties, compare targeting health: the lower value of log2(current HP) + Defense / 100 is preferred.
  4. A hidden identity resolves a remaining exact tie, so avoid perfect ties when first contact matters.

Place heroes in job order

PlacementCheckCommon correction
AnchorIs it strictly closer to the opening threat?Move one hex forward or into the threatened lane
CarryCan it attack without wasting the opening?Clear its route or use the correct row
SupportDoes its range cover the intended allies?Move closer without becoming second contact
Flex heroDoes it answer this exact formation?Swap with reserve instead of rebuilding the core

The front row is y=3 and the back row is y=0. Adjacent means a hex distance of 1. When a modifier depends on a row or nearby ally, confirm the board coordinate rather than how close the characters look. Pathing and attack locks are separate: a unit can prefer one target, fall back when blocked, and keep a locked attack once it starts.

Shop and Shard economy

Rerolls, heroes, items, and relics compete for the same economy. A rare-looking offer is not automatically correct. Buy the effect that fixes the next fight or deepens a trigger the team already produces.

What a regular shop contains

After a normal win, a regular shop offers three heroes, two items, and one relic. One random offer is discounted by 25%. The first reroll costs 1 Shard and each later reroll during the same visit costs 1 more. Freeze carries useful offers into the next regular shop.

OfferPriceBefore buying
HeroC 15 · B 25 · A 35 · S 45Does the recruit fill a job or create the next rank?
ItemCommon 5 · Rare 15 · Epic 25Which holder and item slot are already available?
RelicCommon 10 · Rare 20 · Epic 30 · Legendary 40How often does the active board trigger it?
Team Size45Is the next active hero ready to field now?

A practical stop rule

  1. Name at least two acceptable reroll outcomes.
  2. Reserve the cost of the next known breakpoint.
  3. Stop after finding the planned role, rank, or trigger.
  4. Freeze only when the exact offer remains useful after another floor.

Heroes and items sell for 66% of their value. Relics cannot be sold. The post-boss Auction House offers three heroes, four items, and three relics, starts rerolls at 7 Shards, and cannot be frozen—enter with a priority order before browsing.

Read a loss instead of restarting the plan

Use Emergency Rewind as a learning attempt. Change one variable—formation, active roster, equipment holder, or purchase—then compare the new opening. If the carry still cannot reach its target, more Attack is unlikely to solve the real problem.

  • Carry dies before the first cast → move the anchor closer or buy frontline protection.
  • Frontline lives but enemies do not fall → open a clean lane or rank the damage dealer.
  • Abilities arrive too late → protect the caster or buy Starting Mana / Attack Speed.
  • Fourth hero adds no value → return the specialist to reserve and finish the three-hero core.

Where to go next

Continue with the strategy guide for ranks, team engines, relics, Red Rift, and Endless. Use the player handbook for combat rules, the growth route for board size and upgrades, and the enemy database when one exact formation stops the run.

title: Guildrun Strategy Guide: Builds, Ranks, Relics and Modes
imageAlt: Guildrun party fighting in a coordinated formation
excerpt: Advanced decision frameworks for team engines, Rank C–S paths, relic evaluation, Red Rift pressure, and Endless scaling in Demo 0.5.1.
author: Guildrun Guide Team
quickSummary: Treat a composition as a repeatable engine, not a fixed roster.
Concentrate ranks until a hero’s next upgrade changes the next fight.
Judge relics by trigger frequency, then adapt the plan for Red Rift and Endless.
commonMistakes: Collecting class tags without a payoff
Ranking every hero evenly
Taking delayed relics before the board is stable
Using an Endless-only plan in Red Rift
Entering Endless with only flat stats
detailsHtml:
How to use this guide

Read the beginner guide first if the opening run still collapses before Act 2. This page assumes you already understand the run loop, then focuses on build identity, progression choices, relic evaluation, and mode-specific pressure for Demo 0.5.1.

Build engines, not fixed rosters

The strongest teams are not collections of individually strong heroes. A coherent composition produces a trigger repeatedly, converts it into value, and survives long enough for that conversion to matter.

PartQuestionWarning sign
TriggerWhat happens several times each fight?Only one hero can start it
PayoffWhat value does each trigger create?The build applies effects but does not win
TimeHow does the team survive until the payoff scales?The engine starts after the frontline dies
AccessCan the right hero reach the right target?Damage is spent on a low-priority body

Practical frameworks

  • Shield and Stall. Durable first contact, repeatable shielding, delayed payoffs.
  • Crit sustain. Fast Duelist or Assassin attacks convert Crit into healing, mana, or durability when the right relics appear.
  • Status control. Poison, Frost, and Burn become strong when several effects reward the same debuff.
  • Rush pressure. Needs immediate target access; a unit that spends the opening walking contributes nothing.

When to pivot

  • Pivot when two or more owned pieces support a different repeatable trigger.
  • Hold the plan when only one shop offer suggests the new theme.
  • Drop a class tag that adds no payoff, protection, or target access.
  • Change positioning before replacing a hero that is failing only because of its lane.

Hero progression: Rank C to S

Guildrun separates hero development inside a run, permanent unlocks across runs, and difficulty progression. Keep those layers distinct so you know what resets and what carries forward.

RankDecisionPick test
CPlace the base hero and confirm its jobCan this hero perform its job with the current formation?
BChoose one of three fixed specializations; some add a second classDoes the path solve today’s fight or unlock an owned interaction?
ADraft the first class modifier from active classesWill this modifier trigger often enough to matter?
STake a second modifier and an extra item slot at Demo maxIs finishing this hero stronger than the next board-size breakpoint?

Do not spread ranks evenly by default. A first Rank B on the main carry or anchor often changes more than giving a weak fourth hero a small bump. Dual-class paths expand later modifier pools, which increases flexibility but can make specific offers less consistent.

Grow the board from three to five active heroes only when the new slot has a job. The roster can hold six for a reserve specialist or Backup interaction. Team Size costs 45 Shards—compare that with the duplicate, item, or relic that would strengthen the current core immediately.

Respec with evidence

  1. Name the current hero’s job.
  2. Identify which part of the specialization no longer activates.
  3. Confirm the replacement path works with owned items and relics.
  4. Reposition before spending on the rebuild.

How to evaluate every relic offer

A relic should be judged by activation frequency, value per trigger, and the probability that the current roster can use it. Relics cannot be sold, so a narrow legendary can be more expensive than its Shard price suggests.

QuestionStrong answerWeak answer
Who triggers it?Two or more active heroesA future recruit you do not own
When does it pay?During the next important fightAfter several unlikely conditions
What does it solve?A named survival or damage failureIt is simply a higher rarity
What does it cost?Fits the next Shard breakpointConsumes the budget for a needed rank

Separate stability from ceiling. Defensive relics can protect a fragile run immediately. Economy and scaling relics may produce a higher ceiling only if the team survives the delay. Quest relics need a realistic completion route: count how often the current board creates the trigger in an ordinary fight before buying the quest.

Exact numbers can move between patches. Re-read the in-game text after a balance update, then filter the relic database or start from a status page to find matching pieces.

Red Rift: mission pressure and safer pivots

Red Rift combines stronger enemies with extra mission pressure. A team that eventually scales in normal play may fail because it loses too many heroes on the way to that ceiling.

  • Value sustain earlier, but prefer sustain that also advances the engine.
  • Treat hero deaths as a resource: a clear can still be strategically poor if it burns the mission allowance.
  • Build the first reliable checkpoint before adding a second fragile carry.
  • Avoid liability units that inflate deaths without changing the fight.
NeedPreferAvoid relying on
Opening stabilityImmediate shields, control, or durable first contactA quest that completes after several risky fights
DamageRepeatable triggers with target accessA carry that spends Rush walking
RecoveryA formation change with a measurable resultRepeating the same board through Rewind
ScalingGrowth that also helps the next checkpointEndless-only ceiling before stabilization

Endless mode: build for repeatable scaling

The normal route asks whether a build can clear the next encounter. Endless asks whether the engine keeps producing more value as enemy health and damage continue to rise.

LayerEndless questionFailure signal
GrowthWhat increases again after another fight?Every bonus is already fixed
SurvivalHow does the team handle larger hits and the anti-stall clock?The frontline only delays defeat
AccessCan damage still reach priority enemies as formations change?The carry is trapped walking or hitting summons
RedundancyWhat happens when the main carry is controlled or blocked?The entire engine stops with one hero

Separate flat power from compounding power. One-time stats can bridge early waves; deep runs need repeatable triggers, permanent-in-run gains, or percent-based defenses. Storm begins at 50 seconds and escalates; Riftbreaker appears at 90 seconds—indefinite survival is not a win condition.

Change one layer at a time

  1. Open the exact stage formation and enemy variants.
  2. Confirm first contact and target access.
  3. Identify whether the loss is damage, survival, control, or scaling.
  4. Replace the weakest engine link, not the highest-stat hero by default.

Connected tools

Use the beginner guide for first-run fundamentals, the growth route for board size and upgrade order, hero dossiers for Rank B paths, fight modes for challenge thresholds, and stage formations when a specific lineup breaks the plan.
